clue.text: Riots ruined most of course! It makes you spit!

indicators.note: riots that are ruined are wrecked, so their letters are knocked into a new order
most of a word means all of it except its final letter

parts.note: a course of lectures or programmes is a series

explanation.surface: A diner exclaims over a meal spoilt by rioting, with a second line about spitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' turns RIOTS into ROTIS; 'most of' drops the last S from SERIES. 'spit' is not the verb but the rod a roast turns on.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotisserie is a cooking device that turns meat on a revolving spit, so it literally makes the spit work.

clue.text: Practised catches in tall grass

indicators.note: in means the word for catches is put inside the word for tall grass

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass growing by water
to catch what someone says is to hear it

explanation.surface: Someone snares things while standing in long grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catches' looks like grabbing but means hears, as in catching a remark.
explanation.definitionFit: To rehearse a performance is to practise it, so practised and rehearsed are synonyms.

clue.text: Hearing of duty, changes course

indicators.note: hearing of means the word for duty is said aloud and taken by sound

parts.note: a duty is a tax on goods

explanation.surface: Hearing about a duty, someone changes their plans.
explanation.walkthrough: In sailing, to tack is to change direction by turning the bow through the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailing boat that tacks swings its bow across the wind to change direction, so it changes course.

clue.text: Collected spades a little person owned

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for spades in card games
an elf is a small creature of folklore
possessed means owned

explanation.surface: Someone gathered spades that belonged to a small person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collected' looks like gathered but is the adjective meaning calm.
explanation.definitionFit: Collected as an adjective means calm and composed, which is what being self-controlled under pressure means.

clue.text: Not, however, one of Hines's titles

definitions.text: Not, however, one of Hines's titles

parts.words: Not, however, one of Hines's titles
parts.note: Earl Hines was an American jazz pianist; his first name is a noble title, yet the rank and territory of a nobleman of that title was never one of his

explanation.surface: A note that something was not among a writer's or musician's titles.
explanation.walkthrough: Earl Hines was a celebrated American jazz pianist nicknamed 'Fatha'; 'titles' suggests his records.
explanation.definitionFit: The rank or territory of a nobleman called an earl, which Hines bore only as a first name.

clue.text: Yours truly's point, at first, regarding painting technique

parts.note: yours truly means I, the speaker, and the 's is am, giving I'm

indicators.note: at first means take the first letter of point

parts.note: as to means regarding

explanation.surface: A speaker explains a point about how a picture is painted.
explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is the technique of laying paint on thickly so brush or knife marks stand out.

clue.text: Son welcomed by primate for recess

indicators.note: something welcomed by another is taken in by it, so the son goes inside the primate

parts.note: an ape is a primate

explanation.surface: A boy is taken in by a monkey and given a place to rest.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is a vaulted recess at the end of a church, so it is a kind of recess.

clue.text: In which, theoretically, capital is spoken of

indicators.note: spoken of means said aloud, so the word for capital is taken by its sound

parts.note: in finance the principal is the capital sum lent or invested

explanation.surface: A remark on a theory in which money is discussed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works as a phrase: 'in ___' means theoretically.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'in principle' means in theory, so the answer is the noun in which something holds theoretically.

clue.text: English fellow rejecting mother's moral code

indicators.note: rejecting means casting out, so the mother is removed from the fellow's name

parts.note: Thomas is a man's name, standing for any fellow
ma is mother, with the possessive giving no letter

explanation.surface: An Englishman turns away from his mother's moral values.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting' takes MA out of THOMAS, leaving THOS.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the guiding beliefs or character of a person or group, i.e. its moral code.

clue.text: Inspector loses head, arresting Liberal barracker

indicators.note: arresting means holding, so the shortened inspector holds the Liberal inside it
losing its head means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: a checker is someone who inspects

explanation.surface: A police inspector in a muddle detains a Liberal heckler at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses head' takes the C off CHECKER, leaving HECKER, and 'arresting' puts L inside it. 'Inspector' suggests a police rank but is only one who checks.
explanation.definitionFit: A barracker shouts down a speaker, which is exactly what a heckler does; the word is common in British and Australian use.

clue.text: Get into print? Damned if I do!

definitions.text: Get into print? Damned if I do!

parts.words: Get into print? Damned if I do!
parts.note: alludes to the Duke of Wellington's reply to a blackmailer, telling him to go ahead and print and be damned; here the would-be author fears damnation for printing

explanation.surface: A writer hesitates over going into print, fearing the consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the famous retort 'Publish and be damned', attributed to the Duke of Wellington when threatened with exposure in a courtesan's memoirs.
explanation.definitionFit: To get something into print is to issue it to the public, which is what the verb means.

clue.text: Beauties about to dip into Latvian's writings

parts.note: belles are beautiful women

indicators.note: to dip into means to go inside, so the word for about goes inside the Latvian's

parts.note: a Lett is a Latvian, and the possessive gives LETT'S
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Beautiful women are about to plunge into a Latvian's books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as 'on the point of' but splits: 'about' is the inserted piece and 'to dip into' the container signal. A Lett is an old name for a Latvian.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means fine writing: literary works valued for style, so writings.

clue.text: Writer's rejected main work

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the word for main is read backwards

parts.note: the main is a poetic name for the sea
OP, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: An author's major work has been turned down by a publisher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns SEA into AES. 'main work' looks like one phrase meaning masterpiece, but 'main' is the sea and 'work' is OP; the 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop was the ancient Greek author to whom the famous fables are credited, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Removes clerk initially paid less when working

indicators.note: working means in operation or reworked, signalling the letters are rearranged
initially means take the first letter of the word clerk

explanation.surface: A clerk is laid off because, once in work, he is paid less.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' gives C from 'clerk'; with PAIDLESS, 'when working' rearranges the nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To displace something is to move it out of its place, so displaces means removes.

clue.text: Even honest dog breeders often do it

definitions.text: Even honest dog breeders often do it

parts.words: Even honest dog breeders often do it
parts.note: the idiom means to swindle someone with a worthless purchase, but literally honest breeders sell young dogs all the time

explanation.surface: A remark that even reputable dog breeders cheat their customers.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is British slang for cheating someone in a sale; read literally, breeders really do sell young dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom literally describes selling a young dog, which breeders do routinely, while its figurative sense is to cheat a buyer.

clue.text: Article, so to speak, by butcher's double

parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang butcher's hook means look
a is the indefinite article
like is the filler used in speech, much as one would say so to speak

explanation.surface: An article about a butcher's twin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' sets the butcher's piece beside the others. Cockney rhyming slang: 'have a butcher's' means have a look.
explanation.definitionFit: A double is a person who closely resembles another, which is what this word means.

clue.text: Mogul's head displayed outside old shelter

indicators.note: displayed outside means the word for head is placed round the other pieces

parts.note: pate is an old word for the head
a tent is a shelter

explanation.surface: A Mughal emperor's head is shown outside an old tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mogul's' reads as possessive but is 'Mogul is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mogul is a powerful magnate or ruler, which is what a potentate is.

clue.text: Make every effort, even stopping Lorna's defeat

indicators.note: stopping means plugging a gap, so the word for even goes inside the other pieces

parts.note: Lorna Doone is the heroine of R. D. Blackmore's novel, so Lorna's gives her surname with the possessive
to best someone is to defeat them
level means even or flat

explanation.surface: Someone tries hard to prevent Lorna from losing a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Lorna Doone is the title heroine of R. D. Blackmore's Victorian romance set on Exmoor, so 'Lorna's' gives her surname; 'even' is the inserted piece, not an adverb.
explanation.definitionFit: To do your utmost is an idiom meaning to try as hard as you possibly can, i.e. to make every effort.

clue.text: Person inclined to embrace one of three basic skills?

definitions.text: Person inclined to embrace one of three basic skills?

indicators.note: to embrace means to hold, so the skill letter goes inside the person inclined

parts.note: a leaner is one who leans, i.e. is inclined
the three Rs are reading, writing and arithmetic, so one of them is R

explanation.surface: Someone keen to take up one of the three Rs.
explanation.walkthrough: The three Rs are reading, writing and arithmetic, the basics of schooling.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone keen to grasp reading, writing or arithmetic is a pupil studying them.

clue.text: Game a cleric is addicted to …

parts.note: Ven is the abbreviation for Venerable, the title of an archdeacon
to be on a drug is to be taking or hooked on it

explanation.surface: A clergyman is hooked on hunting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' means wild animals as meat, not a pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Venison is deer meat, and deer are game animals hunted for food.

clue.text: Seaman who has a pipe with a mate?

definitions.text: Seaman who has a pipe with a mate?

parts.words: Seaman who has a pipe with a mate?
parts.note: suggests a sailor smoking with a friend, but the ship's petty officer in charge of rigging blows a whistle called a pipe and has an assistant called his mate

explanation.surface: A sailor shares a smoke with his friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The pipe is the whistle used to pass orders on deck, and 'mate' is the official title of his deputy.
explanation.definitionFit: This petty officer is a seaman responsible for rigging and deck crew, famous for his whistle and his named assistant.

clue.text: … but an Irish painter may be rasher

definitions.meaning: Francis ..., the Dublin-born painter of distorted figures
a rasher is a thin slice of cured pork

explanation.surface: An Irish artist may be rather rash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rasher' looks like 'more rash' but is a slice of cured meat; the ellipsis links to the game clue above.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon was a Dublin-born painter, and a rasher is a slice of cured pig meat.

clue.text: In effect it antagonised a primordial god

indicators.note: In means the letters are found inside the run of words effect it antagonised

explanation.surface: A remark that something angered an ancient deity.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titans were the elder gods born of Earth and Sky, ruling before the Olympians.

clue.text: Fuss about name written round painting

indicators.note: about means the word for fuss surrounds the abbreviation for name

parts.note: a to-do is a fuss

explanation.surface: A row breaks out over a name signed on a picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' looks like part of 'written round' but belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tondo is a circular painting or relief, from the Italian for round.

clue.text: Caught lying low, having been told off earlier?

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
something lying low is hidden away

explanation.surface: Someone stays out of sight after being scolded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'earlier' signals the dated form: this past participle of chide is old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: Chide means scold, and this archaic past participle means scolded, so told off in older English.

clue.text: Incomplete spraying device found beside a shrub

indicators.note: incomplete means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a syringe squirts liquid in a jet

explanation.surface: A gardener finds a broken sprayer next to a bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incomplete' cuts the E off SYRINGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Syringa is the botanical name of the lilac and also used for mock orange, both garden shrubs.

clue.text: Boy 18's lack of identification around East?

indicators.note: around means the identification phrase goes round the letter for East

parts.note: 18 down is a learner driver, identified by an L plate, so having no L means lacking that identification

explanation.surface: A lad without his ID plates wanders about in the east.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a learner driver must display L plates; a learner without them is 'no L'. 'around' puts E inside NOL.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel is a male first name, so it stands for a boy in crossword terms.

clue.text: It could sharpen the nose of a hard worker

definitions.text: It could sharpen the nose of a hard worker

parts.words: It could sharpen the nose of a hard worker
parts.note: a hard worker keeps their nose to a sharpening stone in the idiom, so taken literally that stone would hone the nose

explanation.surface: A joke that something might make a diligent worker's nose pointy.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'keep your nose to the ___' means to work hard without a break.
explanation.definitionFit: A revolving stone wheel used to sharpen blades, which in the idiom is where a hard worker's nose is kept.
